Whether a prior density has deterministic provenance

Source: R/prior-density-ordinate.R
prior_density_has_provenance.Rd

prior_density_has_provenance() tells whether the prior measure of x is available from deterministic provenance, so that its density heights, ordinate values and region probabilities are evaluated by BayesTools (from structural routes, or from numerical grids refined under error control). It is the public signal for densities without such provenance, whose region probabilities a caller has to obtain in another way (e.g. from prior draws).

prior_density_has_provenance(x)

Arguments

x

A BayesTools prior or prior_linear_density object.

Value

TRUE or FALSE.

Details

A BayesTools prior object is its own provenance. A prior_linear_density has provenance when its builder recorded the prior measure it describes (every density built by the BayesTools prior-density builders, e.g. JAGS_formula_prior_density(), parameter_prior_density() and the prior densities of marginal_posterior()), unless that measure contains a multiply_by product without a structural density route. It has none when it is a numerical density grid without that record (e.g. the standard-deviation components of nested variance allocations) or such a product: both are used for plotting only, and their heights and region probabilities stop. A density of point masses only is exact without a record.

Provenance does not make an ordinate exact: a combination without a structural route (e.g. three non-normal terms) has provenance and refined grid region probabilities, while its ordinates are "unknown", so point hypotheses need prior_ordinate_status(). The method field of prior_density_ordinate() does not separate the cases: it is "unsupported_provenance" for a grid without provenance and for a combination without a structural route alike, and "named_transform" for such a combination under an output transformation.

See also

prior_density_ordinate(), prior_ordinate_status()

Examples

prior_density_has_provenance(prior("normal", list(mean = 0, sd = 1)))
#> [1] TRUE
